paragraphs: Let us see if this idea is right. I think most people will agree with me. Until now, no country has had a perfect life for everybody, as far as we know. There has always been something that stopped people from marrying young. Poor people were afraid that they could not feed their families. Rich people were afraid that they would lose their high place in society. So in every country that we know, the number of people has never been free to grow as fast as it can.

Maybe there is a law about marriage, and maybe there is not. But nature and good morals both seem to say the same thing: a man should love one woman, and early in life. Perhaps people can change partners after a bad choice. But this freedom will not change the number of people much, unless it becomes very bad behaviour. And we are now imagining a society where almost nobody behaves badly.

So imagine a country where people are equal and good. Their way of life is simple and honest. There is so much food that nobody is afraid to have a big family. Here, nothing stops the number of people from growing. In this country, the number of people will clearly grow much faster than ever before.

Let us look at the United States of America. There, people have more food than in any modern country in Europe. Their way of life is more honest. So fewer things stop them from marrying young. In the United States, the number of people has doubled in twenty-five years.

This is not the fastest possible growth. But it comes from real life, so we will use it as our rule. We will say this: when nothing stops it, the number of people doubles every twenty-five years. This kind of growth is called geometrical. The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
Now let us take a piece of land, for example this Island, where I live. How fast can the food from this land grow? We will start with the farms as they are today.

Imagine the best possible government. It gives more land to farmers and helps farming in every way. Perhaps the food from the Island can double in the first twenty-five years. I think this is the most that anybody can ask.

In the next twenty-five years, the food cannot become four times bigger. We know too much about land to believe this. The most we can imagine is this: in the second twenty-five years, the food may grow by the same amount that the Island makes today. Let us use this as our rule, even if it is surely too high. With a lot of hard work, every twenty-five years the Island will make more food. The extra food will be the same amount that it makes now. Even the most hopeful person cannot imagine more than this. After a few hundred years, every piece of land on the Island will look like a garden.
